title: Heat water with a wood stove coil or water jacket
summary: A coil or jacket in the firebox can heat a tank of water by thermosiphon, with no pump. Without an open vent or a working relief valve that nothing can shut off, it becomes a steam bomb when the flow stops. It can also upset a clean-burning stove, with more emissions and creosote.

materials.item: Water coil or jacket made for the stove, or a kit coil
Hot-water storage tank: an open-vented cylinder, or an old water-heater tank
Copper pipe, ¾ to 1 in (20 to 25 mm), and fittings
Copper vent pipe, at least 20 mm, for an open-vented layout
Listed temperature-and-pressure relief valve (CSA, ANSI Z21.22), with full-size discharge pipe
materials.qty: 1 per tank, plus 1 at the coil

materials.item: Tempering (mixing) valve for the hot outlet
High-temperature rope gasket, locknuts and washers for the coil legs
Pipe insulation for any vent or pipe that could freeze
Drain valve at the lowest point

steps.text: Decide whether a pot on the stove will do. A coil is complicated, cools the fire and can make more creosote; NRCan wants one certified for the stove (NRCan wood heating, Level wetbacks).
Pick the layout: a tank with an open vent pipe to the air, or a pressurised water-heater tank with a working T&P relief valve at its top (ADG Wales, NZ G12, North coil kit).
steps.warn: A coil on a closed loop with no vent and no relief valve becomes a steam bomb when the flow stops (CPSC fireplace water heaters, NRCan wood heating).

steps.text: Use a coil or jacket made and certified for the stove where you can (NRCan wood heating). A kit coil follows its own maker's instructions. The North kit is for a cook stove: its coil lies horizontally over the firebricks under the cooktop, not inside the firebox, with its legs through holes drilled in the stove wall and sealed with locknuts, washers and fibreglass rope gasket, and its sheet says to use a licensed plumber (North coil kit).
steps.warn: Don't centre-punch cast iron: it cracks. Mark it with a pen (North coil kit).

steps.text: Set the tank within about 3 m (10 ft) of the stove, with the top of the tank, where its relief valve sits, higher than the coil's top leg (North coil kit); Level says to keep the tank close to the heat (Level wetbacks).
steps.warn: A full tank is heavy. Welsh guidance stands a cold-water cistern on a flat, level, rigid platform able to carry it full to the rim (ADG Wales): do the same.

steps.text: Run copper pipe, ¾ to 1 in (20 to 25 mm), from the coil's top leg rising to the top of the tank, with an automatic air vent at the high point. Run the cold return from the tank's bottom to the coil's bottom leg (North coil kit, Level wetbacks, NZ G12).
steps.warn: Never plastic tube between the coil and the tank: it can melt (North coil kit).

steps.text: Open-vented layout: run a vent pipe of at least 20 mm from the top of the tank to end outdoors or over the cold-water supply tank, open to the air (NZ G12, ADG Wales). Insulate it where it could freeze (NZ G12).

Pressurised layout: fit a listed T&P valve with its probe in the top 152 mm (6 in) of the tank, its discharge rating above the heat going in, opening at 99 °C (210 °F) and at the tank's rated working pressure (Watts LF100XL, North coil kit, BC Plumbing Code 2.6.1.7).
Fit a relief valve in the coil's outlet pipe as close to the coil as you can (CPSC fireplace water heaters).
steps.warn: No valve or restriction between the coil and its relief valve or vent, ever (CPSC fireplace water heaters, Woodfire Passiv).

steps.text: Pipe every relief valve full size, sloping down, to end at least 150 mm (6 in) above a drain where you can see it (Watts LF100XL).
steps.warn: Never cap or connect anything to a relief outlet (North coil kit). It discharges scalding water and steam (ADG Wales).

steps.text: Fit a mixing (tempering) valve on the hot outlet and set it to 49 °C (120 °F) (Parachute hot tap water, GoC water temperature). A stove can push the tank to 82 to 88 °C (180 to 190 °F) (North coil kit), and 60 °C can give a child a third-degree burn in about a second (Parachute hot tap water).

Fill the tank and coil completely and bleed the air out before the first fire. Light only when the coil and pipes are full, open and not frozen (Woodfire Passiv asks for a free flow of water before lighting).
Test each relief valve by lifting its lever once before the first fire and at least once a year after, standing clear of the outlet (Watts LF100XL, CPSC fireplace water heaters).
steps.warn: No water from the outlet means the valve is stuck: don't fire the stove until it is replaced (Watts LF100XL).

steps.text: If it knocks, hisses or the relief valve opens, turn the air down, add no wood and let the fire burn down (Woodfire Passiv does this when its overheat valve keeps running). Keep clear of vents and outlets: they discharge scalding water and steam (ADG Wales).

If the coil boiled dry, let the stove and coil cool right down before any water goes back in (Weil-McLain EGH, CEA low water). Don't open any valve that would feed water in, and find out why the flow stopped before you refill (CEA low water).
steps.warn: Never put cold water into a hot boiler (CEA low water). It can crack the metal (Weil-McLain EGH), and water turning to steam takes about 1,600 times the space (National Board bomb).

steps.text: Before a freeze with the stove out, drain the coil, tank and pipes (Get Prepared outages, CPSC fireplace water heaters). Before the stove is lit again, refill and bleed them, and check nothing is frozen (Woodfire Passiv, CPSC fireplace water heaters).

notes:
## Is it worth it?
A coil or water jacket in a firebox heats water with no pump: hot water rises out of the coil to a tank above and cooler water sinks back in (Level wetbacks). New Zealand wetbacks give about 1.5 to 4 kW to the water (Level wetbacks). The costs:
- NRCan calls domestic hot-water coils rarely feasible, complicated and, when badly designed, dangerous: with no proper pressure relief, trapped steam can cause a violent explosion. It wants the coil certified for that stove and installed exactly to the maker's instructions (NRCan wood heating).
- The coil takes heat out of the stove: Level says a jacket reduces the heat output to the room. NRCan warns it can raise emissions and creosote in a clean-burning stove, and in New Zealand some burners pass the efficiency test without a wetback and fail with one (NRCan wood heating, Level wetbacks). Check the chimney more often: [Chimney sweeping](#guides/skill_chimney_sweeping).

If you can heat water in a pot on the stove top instead, that has no pressure to go wrong: [Cook on a wood stove](#guides/skill_cook_on_wood_stove).

## Why coils explode
If the flow through a coil slows or stops (a failed pump, a power cut, frozen pipes), the water in it can boil into steam (CPSC fireplace water heaters). A shut valve stops the flow the same way, which is why CPSC wants no valve or restriction between the coil and its relief valve. With no working relief device the pressure builds until something bursts (CPSC fireplace water heaters). Water flashing to steam needs about 1,600 times the space, and the National Board of boiler inspectors works out that a 30 US gal (114 L) home water tank failing at 166 °C (332 °F) releases enough energy to throw a car about 38 m (125 ft) into the air; a working temperature-and-pressure relief valve would prevent that failure (National Board bomb).

So every safe layout comes down to two things: **the coil can always vent to the air or through a relief valve, and nothing can shut that path.**

## Two safe layouts
| Layout | What keeps it safe | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Open-vented** (UK and NZ practice) | A vent pipe from the top of the tank, or from the coil's flow pipe, open to the air above the cold-water tank's water level. Welsh (UK) guidance: at least 19 mm inside, plus a temperature relief valve or cut-out. NZ: copper, at least 20 mm where input is over 3 kW, ending outdoors or over the supply tank | ADG Wales, NZ G12 |
| **To a pressurised water-heater tank** (North American kits) | A working temperature-and-pressure (T&P) relief valve at the top of the tank, its probe in the top 152 mm (6 in), rated above the coil's heat; plus a relief valve at the coil if any valve or pump is in the loop | North coil kit, Watts LF100XL, CPSC fireplace water heaters |

NZ's code connects wetbacks only to open-vented heaters or a storage vessel, and calls for a heat exchanger where the tank runs at higher pressure than the open-vented wetback circuit (NZ G12). A coil plumbed into a closed loop with neither a vent nor a relief valve is the steam bomb.

## Pipes and heights for thermosiphon
- **Tank close and high.** One kit wants the tank less than 3 m (10 ft) from the stove, with the top of the tank, where the T&P valve sits, higher than the coil's top leg; raise the tank if needed (North coil kit). Keep the tank near the heat source (Level wetbacks).
- **Big pipe, rising.** 25 mm wetback pipes are recommended for flow, and some makers give a minimum gradient for the hot pipe up to the tank (Level wetbacks). The North kit uses ¾ in (about 20 mm) copper with an automatic float air vent at the high point (North coil kit); a UK boiler stove wants 28 mm on its heat-leak loop so it can thermosiphon (Woodfire Passiv).
- **Copper, not plastic.** NZ's code asks for a copper wetback and copper pipe to the tank (NZ G12); plastic tube near a stove can melt (North coil kit).
- **Hot from the top of the coil to the top of the tank; cold from the bottom of the tank back to the bottom of the coil** (North coil kit).
- **A salvaged water-heater tank** can hold the water. North calls an old tank without its electrical connections ideal for this (North coil kit), so take out or disconnect any elements and thermostat, and pick the relief valve to suit the tank's rated working pressure (BC Plumbing Code 2.6.1.7).

## Relief valves
- Use a listed T&P valve, such as Watts LF100XL: CSA listed, ANSI Z21.22, opens at 99 °C (210 °F), standard pressure settings 75, 100, 125 or 150 psi (1,034 kPa for 150), rated up to 105,000 BTU/h (about 31 kW). Its discharge rating must exceed the heat going into the water, it is for emergencies and not a thermostat, and it wants a look for scale at least every three years (Watts LF100XL). The Watts sheet says nothing about a stove coil's output: NZ jackets are listed at 1.5 to 4 kW (Level wetbacks), so check yours. The valve should open at the tank's rated working pressure, so read the tank's plate before choosing (BC Plumbing Code 2.6.1.7).
- Its pipe stays full size all the way, slopes down, and ends at least 150 mm (6 in) above a drain where you can see it run (Watts LF100XL). Never connect anything to the outlet (North coil kit). What comes out is scalding water and steam (ADG Wales). In British Columbia's plumbing code the pipe ends over a floor drain with an air break of no more than 300 mm, and no shut-off valve may sit between the tank and its relief valves (BC Plumbing Code 2.6.1.7); the Watts sheet's 150 mm is the least.
- Lift the lever at least once a year, standing clear: mineral scale can jam a valve shut, and no flow means it is dead (Watts LF100XL, CPSC fireplace water heaters).
- **No valves or restrictions between the coil and its relief valve** (CPSC fireplace water heaters, Woodfire Passiv). The relief valve goes in the outlet pipe as close to the coil as you can (CPSC fireplace water heaters).

## Pumps and power cuts
A pumped loop stops when the power does, and CPSC lists power outages among the ways flow halts (CPSC fireplace water heaters). Where a kit uses a pump and a gate valve, it puts a second T&P valve right on the coil's top leg (North coil kit). One boiler-stove maker sets its pump unit so water keeps circulating by gravity round a "heat leak" radiator in a power failure, piped in 28 mm so it can thermosiphon (Woodfire Passiv). Some boiler stoves add an overheat valve that runs mains water through a cooling coil, but it needs at least 2 bar and 900 L/h from a supply that can't be shut off (Woodfire Passiv), so with no mains it does nothing: build for gravity.

## Fire, CO and the chimney
NRCan warns that a coil can degrade a clean-burning stove, giving high emissions and creosote (NRCan wood heating). Sweep the chimney more often, and keep a working CO alarm and smoke alarm in the room: [Install a salvaged wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install), [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide). The tank, its jacket, any foam or plastic on its pipes, and the shelf or frame it stands on need checking too: anything that burns stays outside the stove's clearances, which is the label's distance or 1,200 mm (48 in) for an unlabelled stove (NRCan wood heating).

## Scalding water
With nothing drawing it off, a stove can push tank water to 82 to 88 °C (180 to 190 °F) (North coil kit). Welsh building guidance calls for a tempering valve on the outlet where stored water can pass 80 °C, so the supply is no hotter than 60 °C, and limits the water to a bath to 48 °C (ADG Wales). The North kit's sheet says to set its valve to 130 °F (54 °C) (North coil kit). Canada's advice is lower still: mixing valves set to 49 °C (120 °F) on faucets, showers and tubs, with the stored water at 60 °C (140 °F) against Legionella (GoC water temperature). At 60 °C a child can get a third-degree burn in about a second, and people who can't feel heat quickly, such as older adults and people with diabetes, are at risk too (Parachute hot tap water). Set the mixing valve to 49 °C, and don't draw a bath or wash a child from the raw tank outlet.

## Freezing
Frozen pipes are one of the ways flow stops (CPSC fireplace water heaters). Insulate any vent pipe that could freeze (NZ G12). If the house will freeze while the stove is out, drain the plumbing (Get Prepared outages), coil and tank included. After the stove has sat cold, don't light it until you know the coil and pipes are full, open and not frozen: Woodfire's manual says not to light its boiler stove after a period of inactivity until water flows freely through the system (Woodfire Passiv). A fire under a coil with ice in it is the steam case CPSC warns of (CPSC fireplace water heaters). If you drained the coil, refill and bleed it before any fire: a dry coil in a lit firebox overheats, and the first water back in meets hot metal (Woodfire Passiv, CEA low water).

## If it boils or runs dry
Knocking, hissing, a spitting vent or a relief valve letting go mean the water is boiling. Turn the air down, add no wood and let the fire burn down (Woodfire Passiv); keep clear of the vent and valve outlets. If the coil boiled dry, **don't** pour or run cold water into it while it's hot: let the stove and coil cool right down first. Boiler makers and operators give the same rule: don't add cold water to a hot boiler, because thermal shock can crack it (Weil-McLain EGH, CEA low water). Those rules are written for gas-fired and industrial boilers, so applying them to a stove coil is a precaution by analogy, not a test of a coil. Water turning to steam takes about 1,600 times the space (National Board bomb). Then find out why the flow stopped before you fire it again.
